title: STL map, set, priority queue & review problems
overview: This module gives you three ready-made STL containers built on trees and heaps: `map` (a sorted key-value store), `set` (sorted unique values) and `priority_queue` (a heap that always shows the biggest or smallest item). You also learn to write a compare class so a priority queue can order your own objects. The practice day reviews linked lists, prefix sums and trees with LeetCode problems.

concepts.explain: Stores pairs sorted by key, like a dictionary. Insert, find and erase are O(log n) because it is a balanced BST inside.
Reading `mp[k]` for a key that is not there quietly inserts it with value 0. Use `mp.count(k)` when you only want to ask whether it exists.
Keeps only unique values, always in ascending order. Great for 'sort and remove duplicates' in one go.
A heap. By default `top()` is the largest value; with `greater<int>` it becomes a min-heap. push and pop are O(log n), top is O(1).
`operator()(l, r)` returns true when `l` should sit **lower** than `r` (come out later). So `l.marks < r.marks` makes the highest marks come out first. This feels reversed compared with `sort`.
concepts.snippet: bool operator()(Student l, Student r){ return l.marks < r.marks; }

concepts.explain: Read the whole line with `getline`, wrap it in a `stringstream`, then `ss >> word` gives one word at a time.
Keep a running left sum; the right sum is `total - left - nums[i]`. This turns an O(n^2) check into O(n).

files.title: STL map basics
files.what: Shows how to fill a `map`, print it two ways, read values by key, and test whether a key exists.
steps: `map<int,int> mp` gets keys 1..5 with values 10..50 using `mp[key] = value`.
The first print loop uses an iterator: `it->first` is the key, `it->second` the value.
The second print loop uses `for(auto &pair : mp)`; the `&` avoids copying each pair.
`map<string,int> mp2` shows keys can be strings; `mp2["abc"]` prints 10.
`mp2["xyz"]` prints 0 and, as a side effect, adds key `xyz` to the map.
`mp2.count(...)` returns 1 or 0, so it is the safe way to check presence.
files.complexity: Each insert/lookup O(log n) · printing all O(n)
files.output_note: Keys 1-5 with their values appear twice (once per loop), then `10`, then `0` for the missing key, then `Key is not present`.
files.watch_out: Using `mp[k]` just to check a key adds that key. Use `count` or `find` for checks.

check.a: 6, because the lookup inserted `xyz` with value 0.

files.title: Count each word with a map
files.what: Reads one line, splits it into words and counts how often each word appears, printing the words in alphabetical order.
steps: `getline(cin, s)` reads the whole line, spaces included.
`stringstream ss(s)` lets `ss >> word` pull out one word at a time.
`mp[word]++` starts a new word at 0 and adds 1, so no special case is needed.
The iterator loop prints each key and its count; the map keeps keys sorted.
files.complexity: Time O(w log w) for w words · Space O(w)
files.input: the cat and the dog and the bird
files.input_note: One line of words separated by spaces.
files.output_note: Words come out alphabetically, not in reading order: `and 2`, `bird 1`, `cat 1`, `dog 1`, `the 3`.
files.watch_out: Words are case-sensitive: `The` and `the` would be counted separately.

check.q: Why does `mp[word]++` work for a word seen for the first time?
check.a: Accessing a missing key creates it with value 0, then `++` makes it 1.

files.title: STL set: sorted and unique
files.what: Inserts n numbers into a `set`, prints them sorted without duplicates, prints them in reverse through a vector, and checks if 4 is present.
steps: Each `s.insert(x)` ignores values already in the set.
Walking from `s.begin()` to `s.end()` gives ascending order (an in-order walk of the BST inside).
To get descending order, the values are copied into vector `v` and `reverse`d.
`s.count(4)` is 1 if 4 is in the set, otherwise 0.
files.complexity: Time O(n log n) · Space O(n)
files.output_note: All on one line: `1 2 4 5 8` (sorted, duplicates gone), then `8 5 4 2 1` (reversed), then `4 is present`.
files.watch_out: No newline is printed between the parts, so the three results run together. Add `cout << endl;` after each loop. (A set can also be walked backwards with `rbegin()`/`rend()`, no vector needed.)

check.q: With input `3` and `9 9 9`, what does the first loop print?
check.a: Just `9`, because a set keeps one copy.

files.title: Max-heap and min-heap with priority_queue
files.what: Pushes and pops numbers in a default (max) priority queue and a `greater<int>` (min) priority queue, printing `top()` after each change.
steps: `priority_queue<int> pq`: after pushing 10, 5, 30 the top is 30.
`pop()` removes 30, so the top becomes 10; pushing 100 makes it 100; pushing 21 does not change it.
`pq.empty()` prints 0 because the queue still has items.
`priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> pq2` keeps the smallest on top: 5, then 10 after a pop.
Pushing 100 and 21 leaves 10 on top; pushing 3 makes 3 the top.
files.output_note: Lines 1-5 (`30 10 100 100 0`) come from the max-heap; lines 6-11 (`5 10 10 10 3 0`) come from the min-heap.
files.watch_out: The comments in the file say the min-heap top is 5 after pushing 100 and 21, but 5 was already popped, so the real output is 10. The last line checks `pq.empty()` again instead of `pq2.empty()`.

check.q: Which template argument turns a priority queue into a min-heap?
check.a: The third one, `greater<int>` (with `vector<int>` as the second).

files.title: Priority queue of students with a compare class
files.what: Stores `Student` objects in a priority queue ordered by marks (high first), breaking ties by roll (small first).
steps: `Student` holds `name`, `roll` and `marks`.
`cmp::operator()(l, r)` returns true when `l` should come out after `r`.
`l.marks < r.marks` returns true, so lower marks sink and higher marks rise to the top.
When marks are equal, `l.roll > r.roll` makes the larger roll sink, so the smaller roll comes out first.
The main loop prints `top()` and pops until the queue is empty.
files.complexity: Time O(n log n) · Space O(n)
files.input_note: n, then n lines of `name roll marks`.
files.output_note: `mina 1 92` comes first (highest marks); `sakib 2 85` beats `rafi 3 85` on the smaller roll; `tuli 4 70` is last.
files.watch_out: The comparator reads the opposite way from `sort`: for `sort`, `a < b` means ascending; for a priority queue it means the biggest comes out first.

check.q: What single change makes the lowest marks come out first?
check.a: Change the first comparison to `l.marks > r.marks` returning true.

files.title: Middle of the linked list

problem.name: LeetCode 876 - Middle of the Linked List

files.what: Counts the nodes, then walks `size / 2` steps from the head to reach the middle (the second middle when the size is even).
steps: `get_size` walks the list once and counts nodes.
`idx = size / 2` is the middle position (0-based).
A second walk moves `temp` forward `idx` times and returns it.
files.input_note: n, then the n list values (LeetCode example 2).
files.output_note: `middle node = 4` and `list from middle: 4 5 6`, matching LeetCode's expected answer [4,5,6]. With 6 nodes, idx = 3, so the second of the two middles is returned.
files.watch_out: A single pass with a slow pointer (1 step) and a fast pointer (2 steps) finds the middle without counting first.

check.q: For a list of 6 nodes, which node (1-based) is returned?
check.a: The 4th, because idx = 6/2 = 3 steps from the head.

files.title: Design a linked list
files.what: Builds a doubly linked list class with `head`, `tail` and `size`, supporting get, add at head/tail/index, and delete at index.
steps: `get` returns -1 for a bad index, otherwise walks `index` steps from `head`.
`addAtHead` and `addAtTail` handle the empty list by pointing both `head` and `tail` at the new node.
`addAtIndex` sends index 0 and index `size` to the head/tail helpers; otherwise it stops at node `index-1` and links the new node after it.
`deleteAtIndex` has four cases: only one node, the first node, the last node, and a middle node (unlinked using `prev` and `next`).
`size` is updated in every add and delete so the bounds checks stay correct.
files.input:
addAtHead 1
addAtTail 3
addAtIndex 1 2
get 1
deleteAtIndex 1
get 1
get 5
files.input_note: One command per line (the LeetCode example, plus `get 5` to test a bad index).
files.output_note: After each change the driver prints the whole list: `1`, `1 3`, `1 2 3`. `get(1) = 2` and, after deleting index 1, `get(1) = 3`, matching LeetCode's expected answers. `get(5) = -1` because index 5 is out of range.
files.watch_out: In `addAtIndex`, `index == size` must go to `addAtTail` before the middle case, or `tmp->next->prev` would touch a NULL pointer.

check.q: Why does keeping a `tail` pointer help?
check.a: `addAtTail` and deleting the last node become O(1) instead of walking the whole list.

files.title: Merge nodes in between zeros

problem.name: LeetCode 2181 - Merge Nodes in Between Zeros

files.what: Sums each group of values between two zeros and stores the sum in the first node of that group, reusing the existing nodes.
steps: `modify` starts at the first node after the leading zero; `nextSum` scans from there.
The inner loop adds values into `sum` until `nextSum` reaches a zero.
`modify->val = sum` writes the group total into the group's first node.
`nextSum` steps past the zero and `modify->next` jumps straight to it, skipping the rest of the group.
After the last zero, `nextSum` is NULL, which ends the loop; the answer starts at `head->next`.
files.input_note: n, then the list values; the list starts and ends with 0 (LeetCode example 1).
files.output_note: `merged: 4 11`: 3+1 = 4 and 4+5+2 = 11, the same as LeetCode's expected [4,11].
files.watch_out: The skipped nodes are never deleted. That is fine on LeetCode but leaks memory in a real program.

files.title: Find pivot index
files.what: Finds the first index where the sum to its left equals the sum to its right, using one total and a running left sum.
steps: The first loop adds everything into `total`.
For each `i`, `rightSum = total - leftSum - nums[i]`.
If `leftSum == rightSum`, return `i` right away (the leftmost pivot).
Otherwise add `nums[i]` to `leftSum` and move on; return -1 if nothing matched.
files.input_note: n, then the n numbers (LeetCode example 1).
files.output_note: `pivotIndex = 3`, as LeetCode expects: left of index 3 is 1+7+3 = 11, right is 5+6 = 11.

check.a: 0, because the left sum is 0 and the right sum is 1 + (-1) = 0.

files.title: Left and right sum differences

problem.name: LeetCode 2574 - Left and Right Sum Differences

files.what: Builds a left-sum array and a right-sum array, then returns `|left[i] - right[i]|` for each position.
steps: `leftSum` starts with 0 (nothing is left of index 0), then grows with running sums up to index n-2.
For every i from 1, an inner loop adds `nums[i..n-1]` to get the right sum of position i-1.
A final 0 is pushed for the last position (nothing is to its right).
`result[i] = abs(leftSum[i] - rightSum[i])`.
files.complexity: Time O(n^2) (inner loop for right sums) · Space O(n)
files.input_note: n, then the n numbers (LeetCode example 1).
files.output_note: `answer: 15 1 11 22`, as LeetCode expects. It comes from left = [0,10,14,22] and right = [15,11,3,0].
files.watch_out: The right sums are recomputed from scratch each time, which is O(n^2). Use `right = total - left - nums[i]` for O(n), as in the pivot-index problem.

check.q: How can you get each right sum in O(1)?
check.a: Compute the total once; the right sum at i is `total - leftSum - nums[i]`.

files.title: Maximum depth of a binary tree

problem.name: LeetCode 104 - Maximum Depth of Binary Tree

files.what: Recursively finds the depth of the left and right subtrees and returns the larger one plus 1.
steps: An empty tree (`root == NULL`) has depth 0.
`l` and `r` are the depths of the two subtrees.
The current node adds one level: `max(l, r) + 1`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(h) for the recursion
files.input_note: Tree values in level order with -1 for a missing child (LeetCode example [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]).
files.output_note: `maxDepth = 3`, as LeetCode expects: the longest path is 3 → 20 → 15 (or 7).

check.q: What is the depth of a tree with only a root?
check.a: 1, because both children give 0 and max(0,0)+1 = 1.

practice_links.name: Search in a Binary Search Tree

recap: `map` = sorted key-value pairs; `set` = sorted unique values; both O(log n) per operation.
`mp[k]` inserts missing keys; use `count` to only check.
`priority_queue` is a max-heap; add `greater<T>` for a min-heap.
In a compare class, returning true means the left item comes out later.
`getline` + `stringstream` is the standard way to split a line into words.
Right sum = total - left sum - current: prefix sums without extra arrays.

check_yourself.q: You need to remove duplicates from a list and print it sorted. Which container does this in one step?
check_yourself.a: `set`, because it stores unique values in ascending order.

check_yourself.q: A max-heap holds 4, 9, 2. You pop once and push 7. What is `top()`?
check_yourself.a: 7. After popping 9 the heap has 4 and 2, and 7 is now the largest.

check_yourself.q: In a student priority queue you want the lower roll first on ties. Which comparison goes in the tie branch?
check_yourself.a: `return l.roll > r.roll;` so the larger roll sinks and the smaller one comes out first.

check_yourself.q: Why is a `map` lookup O(log n) and not O(1)?
check_yourself.a: It is a balanced binary search tree, so a search follows one path from the root down.
